meaning: B is only possible because of A; without A, there would be no B. Stresses that A is an essential precondition.

senses.label: No B without A
senses.meaning: A is a necessary condition for B to exist. Like “B is only possible thanks to A” or “without A, there is no B”. Often carries gratitude toward A or a sense that A matters most.
senses.connection: Noun A + あっての + Noun B (e.g. 「お客様あっての商売」, 「健康あっての仕事」)
examples: A business only exists because of its customers, so I want to take good care of our service.
You can only work if you're healthy. Don't push yourself too hard.
Life comes first. Stay away from anything dangerous.

senses.label: Sentence-final 「あってのこと」
senses.meaning: 「Aあってのことだ」 at the end of a sentence says that a result was only achieved thanks to A. Common when thanking people or looking back on an achievement.
senses.connection: Noun + あってのこと（だ／です）
examples: This success is entirely thanks to everyone's cooperation.
I am who I am today only because of my family's support.

notes: A is usually something seen as fundamental, such as customers, health, support, or effort. B is often work, business, or success.
In 「理由があってのこと」, the 「あって」 after 「が」 is just the verb “to exist”: “there must be a reason”. That is not this pattern.
「命あっての物種」 is a set proverb: “as long as you're alive, everything is possible”.

daily.title: Telling a friend to look after themselves
daily.description: Your friend has been working overtime day after day, and you tell them not to overdo it.
daily.example: You can only work if your body holds up, so take a little break.

daily.title: Watching an interview
daily.description: An athlete thanks their supporters in a medal interview.
daily.example: This gold medal is all thanks to the support of my fans.

work.title: A manager talks to the staff
work.description: Stressing that customers are the foundation of everything.
work.example: Please never forget that this store only exists because of our customers.

work.title: Speech at a project celebration
work.description: The project lead thanks the team.
work.example: The project's success is entirely thanks to the hard work of every team member.

etymology: Made from 「あって」 (the te-form of 「ある」) plus the particle 「の」. Literally “B that comes after having A”, which became “B exists only because of A”.

similar.title: 〜なくして（は）
similar.explanation: 「Aなくして（は）Bない」 says it from the negative side: “without A, B is impossible”. 「AあってのB」 says it from the positive side: “B exists thanks to A”. Same idea, opposite direction.

similar.title: 〜てこそ
similar.explanation: 「〜てこそ」 follows an action: “only by doing ... can you ...”. 「あっての」 follows a noun and presents the existence of A as the precondition.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: 「からこそ」 emphasizes a reason: “precisely because ...”. 「あっての」 emphasizes an indispensable precondition.

meaning: Things change depending on the content or state of A. Like “depending on A” or “it all comes down to A”.
connection: Noun（の） + いかんで／いかんでは／いかんによって（は）／いかんだ

senses.label: Depending on ...
senses.meaning: The outcome varies with A. Like “depends on A” or “is determined by A”. A stiff, written version of 「〜次第で」.
senses.connection: Noun（の） + いかんで／いかんによって／いかんだ (e.g. 「結果いかんで」, 「努力のいかんによって」)
examples: Whether you pass is decided by how the interview goes.
Whether you succeed or not depends on your own effort.
We will change the venue depending on the number of participants.

senses.label: Depending on ..., possibly ...
senses.meaning: 「いかんでは／いかんによっては」 means “depending on how A turns out, a certain result is also possible”. What follows is usually an unusual or unwelcome possibility.
senses.connection: Noun（の） + いかんでは／いかんによっては + possible outcome
examples: Depending on the test results, surgery may be necessary.
Depending on how future negotiations go, we may even end the contract.

notes: Very formal. Common in announcements, news, and business documents. In speech, people usually say 「〜次第で」 or 「〜によって」.
It can be written in kanji as 「如何」, but kana 「いかん」 is usual.
「いかんにかかわらず／いかんを問わず」 means the opposite: “regardless of A”.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report on where an election or negotiation is heading.
daily.example: Depending on the election results, a change of government is possible.

daily.title: At the hospital
daily.description: A doctor explains the treatment plan to a patient.
daily.example: Depending on your symptoms, we may need to admit you to the hospital.

work.title: Company notice
work.description: HR explains how bonuses relate to performance.
work.example: The bonus amount will be decided based on performance.

work.title: Contract terms
work.description: What happens if the other party breaches the contract.
work.example: Depending on the seriousness of the breach, the contract may be terminated.

etymology: 「いかん」 comes from 「いかに（如何に）」 + 「ある」: 「いかにある」 became 「いかん」, meaning “how is it?”. In kanji it is 「如何」. Noun + 「いかん」 means “how A turns out”, and adding 「で」 or 「によって」 marks it as the basis for something.

similar.title: 〜次第で (depending on)
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning. 「次第で」 works in both speech and writing; 「いかんで」 is stiffer and mostly used in formal documents.

similar.title: 〜によっては
similar.explanation: 「によっては」 means “in some cases ...” and sounds fairly ordinary. 「いかんによっては」 is more formal and stresses that it depends on the content or degree of A.

similar.title: 〜いかんにかかわらず
similar.explanation: 「いかんで」 means “depending on A”; 「いかんにかかわらず」 means “regardless of A”. They are opposites.

meaning: The result stays the same no matter what the content or state of A is. Like “regardless of A” or “no matter what A is”.
connection: Noun（の） + いかんにかかわらず／いかんによらず／いかんを問わず

senses.label: Regardless of ...
senses.meaning: Whatever A turns out to be, the second part does not change. Stiff and formal. Often used with 「理由」, 「結果」, or 「事情」.
senses.connection: Noun（の） + いかんにかかわらず／いかんによらず (e.g. 「理由のいかんにかかわらず」)
examples: Unexcused absences will not be accepted, whatever the reason.
Regardless of the exam results, everyone will receive a certificate of completion.
Whatever the circumstances, we ask that you meet the deadline.

senses.label: Without regard to ...
senses.meaning: 「いかんを問わず」 means the same. Literally “without asking how A is”. Common in rules, notices, and terms and conditions.
senses.connection: Noun（の） + いかんを問わず
examples: For any reason whatsoever, fees once paid cannot be refunded.
Anyone may apply, regardless of nationality.

notes: Mostly used in written language such as regulations, contracts, and notices. In speech, people usually say 「〜に関係なく」 or 「〜にかかわらず」.
「かかわらず」 can also be written 「関わらず」 or 「拘わらず」.
The noun before it is usually one whose content can vary, such as 「理由」, 「結果」, 「事情」, or 「内容」.

daily.title: A store notice
daily.description: A shop's posted return policy.
daily.example: Regardless of the condition of the item, we cannot accept returns.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report on how a company will deal with misconduct.
daily.example: The company announced it would take strict action, whatever the reason.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: Written rules from the HR department.
work.example: Regardless of the reason, anyone absent without notice for three days or more will be subject to disciplinary action.

work.title: Job posting
work.description: Explaining who can apply.
work.example: Regardless of age or experience, motivated people are welcome.

etymology: 「いかん」 (如何) means “how”. Add 「にかかわらず」 (“unrelated to”), 「を問わず」 (“without asking”), or 「によらず」 (“not depending on”), and you get “no matter how A is”.

similar.title: 〜にかかわらず
similar.explanation: 「にかかわらず」 often follows pairs of opposites like 「晴雨」 or 「男女」. 「いかんにかかわらず」 follows nouns with variable content like 「理由」 or 「結果」, and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜を問わず
similar.explanation: 「を問わず」 attaches directly to nouns like 「年齢」 or 「男女」. 「いかんを問わず」 stresses “whatever the specific content of A is”.

similar.title: 〜いかんで（は）
similar.explanation: 「いかんで」 means “depending on A”, the opposite of this pattern.

meaning: No matter what happens in the first part, the second part is not affected. Like “even if ...” or “no matter ...”.
connection: Verb volitional form + が／と; い-adjective 「〜かろう」 + が／と; Noun / な-adjective + だろう／であろう + が／と

senses.label: Even if ...
senses.meaning: Supposes a situation and says that even so, the second part will not change. Stronger and more determined than 「〜ても」.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form (降ろう・言おう・されよう) + が／と; adjective 「高かろう」 + が／と
examples: Even if it rains tomorrow, the game will go ahead.
No matter how expensive it is, I have no choice but to buy what I need.
Even if the people around me oppose it, I'll go my own way.

senses.label: No matter who / what
senses.meaning: Paired with question words like 「誰」, 「何」, 「どこ」, or 「どんなに」 to mean “no matter who / what / where ...”.
senses.connection: Question word … Verb volitional form + が／と; Question word + だろう／であろう + が／と
examples: No matter who says what, my feelings won't change.
Whoever my opponent is, I won't go easy on them.
Wherever you go is up to you.

senses.label: Whether A or B
senses.meaning: 「Aようが Bようが」 lists two (often opposite) situations and says it makes no difference which one it is.
senses.connection: Aようが（ようと） + Bようが（ようと）; Nounだろうが + Nounだろうが
examples: Come rain or come shine, I'll definitely go.
Child or adult, everyone should follow the rules.

senses.label: Do as you like
senses.meaning: Followed by 「構わない」, 「勝手だ」, or 「関係ない」 to mean “it doesn't matter to me” or “suit yourself”. Sounds indifferent or permissive.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + と（が） + 構わない／勝手だ／関係ない
examples: Whether he quits the company or not has nothing to do with me.
You can eat whatever you like, but take care of your health.

notes: More formal and forceful than 「〜ても」. The second part is usually the speaker's resolve, opinion, or an “I don't care” attitude.
「〜(よ)うが」 and 「〜(よ)うと」 mean nearly the same. 「〜ようとも」 is even more literary.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ようとする」 (try to) or 「〜ようと思う」 (intend to). This pattern is usually followed by a comma or a contrast.
In 「高いだろうが、買う価値はある」, 「だろうが」 means “it's probably ..., but”. That is not this pattern.

daily.title: Declaring your resolve
daily.description: Telling a friend you'll stick with it no matter what.
daily.example: No matter what anyone says to me, I won't give up on this dream.

daily.title: Parent to child
daily.description: Letting a stubborn child decide for themselves.
daily.example: Whether you play or study, decide for yourself.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character declares their determination.
daily.example: Even if I have to make an enemy of the whole world, I'll protect you.

work.title: A boss stresses the rules
work.description: A manager stresses to their team how strict the rules are.
work.example: Whatever the circumstances, please meet the deadline.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator gives an opinion on a policy.
work.example: However loud the opposition is, the government intends to push ahead with the plan.

etymology: Formed from the volitional auxiliary 「う／よう」 plus the conjunctive particle 「が」 (contrast) or 「と」 (supposition). In classical Japanese, 「〜うとも」 expressed a concessive supposition, and modern Japanese keeps it as a strong, formal “even if”.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: 「〜ても」 is the most ordinary way to say “even if”. 「〜(よ)うが／と」 is more formal and forceful, and often goes with question words or statements of resolve.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うが〜まいが
similar.explanation: 「〜ようが〜まいが」 lists only “doing” and “not doing”. This pattern can be used alone or list any two situations.

similar.title: 〜にしろ・〜にせよ
similar.explanation: 「にしろ」 also means “even if”, but it follows the plain form. 「(よ)うが」 uses the volitional form and sounds tougher.

similar.title: 〜とも (concessive)
similar.explanation: 「〜とも」 usually follows the adverbial form of adjectives or the volitional form (「遅くとも」, 「どんなに辛くとも」) and sounds more classical.

meaning: Lists both doing and not doing (or being and not being) and says the result is the same either way. Like “whether or not ...”.
connection: Verb volitional form + が + Verb dictionary form + まいが (〜ようと〜まいと)

senses.label: Whether you do or not
senses.meaning: The same verb appears in the affirmative (volitional form) and negative (まい), meaning the second part is the same whether you do it or not. The second part is usually the speaker's judgment or attitude.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + が + same verb dictionary form + まいが (行こうが行くまいが／食べようが食べまいが／しようがしまいが)
examples: Whether you go or not, I'm going.
Believe it or not, this is a true story.
Whether he joins or not, the plan won't change.

senses.label: Whether it is or not
senses.meaning: With adjectives or nouns, use 「〜かろうと〜なかろうと」 or 「〜であろうとなかろうと」 to say it makes no difference whether something has a certain quality.
senses.connection: Noun / な-adjective + であろうと（が） + なかろうと（が）; い-adjective 「〜かろうと〜なかろうと」
examples: Experienced or not, everyone has to take the test.
Whether you like it or not, you have to do what needs to be done.

notes: The same verb is normally used in both halves. For 「来る」: 「来ようが来まいが／来ようが来るまいが」. For 「する」: 「しようがしまいが／しようがするまいが」.
「〜(よ)うと〜まいと」 means the same as 「〜(よ)うが〜まいが」.
The second part is often 「関係ない」, 「自由だ」, or 「変わらない」.

daily.title: Arguing with a friend
daily.description: Making your position clear to a friend who can't decide.
daily.example: Whether you come or not, the party's going ahead as planned.

daily.title: Parent to child
daily.description: Reminding a child that homework must be done.
daily.example: Whether you feel like it or not, finish your homework today.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A commentator talks about how the weather will affect an event.
daily.example: Rain or no rain, the tournament is scheduled to go ahead.

work.title: Speaking in a meeting
work.description: A manager explains that the plan won't change because of one factor.
work.example: Whether the client approves or not, we should move ahead with the preparations.

work.title: Explaining company rules
work.description: HR explains that training is mandatory.
work.example: Whether you have experience or not, you must attend the new employee training.

etymology: Formed by placing the volitional 「〜(よ)う」 and the negative auxiliary 「まい」 side by side, each followed by 「が／と」: “even if you do, even if you don't”. Neither case affects the result.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うが／〜(よ)うと
similar.explanation: 「〜ようが」 can be used alone or list any two situations. 「〜ようが〜まいが」 specifically contrasts doing vs. not doing.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うか〜まいか
similar.explanation: 「〜ようか〜まいか」 expresses hesitation, “whether to do it or not” (often with 「迷う」). 「〜ようが〜まいが」 means “it's the same either way”.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ
similar.explanation: 「〜にしろ〜にしろ」 lists any two items. 「〜ようが〜まいが」 only lists the affirmative and negative of the same action.

meaning: If you were to do something, it would cause serious trouble. Like “if you dare to ..., you'll be in big trouble”.
connection: Verb volitional form + ものなら

senses.label: If you ever ..., there'll be trouble
senses.meaning: Supposes that someone does something (usually something they shouldn't), and the second part is a serious or troublesome result. Sounds like a warning or a worry.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + ものなら + bad result (e.g. 「〜たら大変だ」, 「〜に違いない」)
examples: If you talk back to that teacher, you'll be in serious trouble.
If you go out in this heavy rain, you'll get soaked.
If this secret ever got out, I couldn't stay at the company.

senses.label: The slightest ... and ...
senses.meaning: Often paired with 「少しでも」, 「ちょっとでも」, or 「一度でも」 to exaggerate: “do even the slightest thing, and there's a huge reaction”. Often used to describe someone's personality or habits.
senses.connection: 少しでも／ちょっとでも + Verb volitional form + ものなら
examples: If I'm even a little late getting home, my dad calls me right away.
Break a promise even once, and she'll never speak to you again.

notes: In casual speech it often becomes 「〜ようもんなら」.
The second part is always a bad result. It cannot express wishes or positive content.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ものなら」 (if one could): 「できるものなら」 follows the potential form and expresses a wish that is hard to realize.

daily.title: Warning a friend
daily.description: Your friend wants to sleep in a strict teacher's class.
daily.example: If you doze off in that class, you'll get kicked out right away.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: Telling a friend how much your mom nags.
daily.example: If my room is even a little messy, my mom lectures me for an hour.

work.title: A senior colleague warns a newcomer
work.description: Warning that a client is very strict.
work.example: If we delay delivery to that client by even one day, they might stop doing business with us.

work.title: Watching the news
work.description: A report on how harsh online opinion can be.
work.example: If a celebrity makes a careless remark, it immediately blows up online.

etymology: Formed from the volitional 「〜(よ)う」, the formal noun 「もの」, and the conditional 「なら」. Literally “if one were to do such a thing”, which came to mean “if you ever did that, then ...”.

similar.title: 〜ものなら
similar.explanation: Potential form + 「ものなら」 expresses a hard-to-reach wish: “if only I could ...”. Volitional form + 「ものなら」 means doing it would lead to a bad result.

similar.title: 〜が最後
similar.explanation: 「が最後」 means once something happens there's no going back, and usually describes an inevitable result. 「ようものなら」 is hypothetical and stresses warning and worry.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 is a neutral conditional. 「ようものなら」 is specifically “if you ever did ...”, and the result is always serious.

meaning: Follows an adjective of emotion to say the speaker's feeling right now is at its peak. Like “extremely ...” or “I couldn't be more ...”.
connection: い-adjective dictionary form / な-adjective + な + 限りだ

senses.label: Extremely (happy, grateful ...)
senses.meaning: Expresses the speaker's strong positive feelings such as joy or gratitude. Only for the speaker's own feelings. Common combinations: 「嬉しい限りだ」, 「心強い限りだ」, 「ありがたい限りだ」.
senses.connection: 嬉しい／ありがたい／心強い／喜ばしい + 限りだ（です）
examples: I couldn't be happier that you've all enjoyed it so much.
Having an experienced senior colleague with me is very reassuring.

senses.label: Extremely (sad, ashamed ...)
senses.meaning: Expresses loneliness, regret, shame, envy, and similar feelings, as in 「寂しい限りだ」, 「残念な限りだ」, 「情けない限りだ」, or 「羨ましい限りだ」.
senses.connection: 寂しい／心細い／情けない／羨ましい + 限りだ; 残念な／不安な + 限りだ
examples: It's so sad that the shop I've gone to for years is closing.
I'm deeply ashamed to have made such a simple mistake.
Being able to travel abroad every year? I'm so jealous.

notes: Only expresses the speaker's own feelings. It is not normally used for a third person's emotions.
It only follows adjectives of feeling or sensation. It cannot follow verbs or ordinary nouns.
In 「本日限り」 (today only) and 「できる限り」 (as much as possible), 「限り」 means “limit”. That is not this pattern.

daily.title: Getting a gift from a friend
daily.description: A friend went out of their way to get you a present.
daily.example: You actually remembered? That makes me so happy.

daily.title: Changes in your hometown
daily.description: You go back home and find a familiar place gone.
daily.example: The park I played in as a kid is gone. It makes me really sad.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A commentator laments school mergers caused by the falling birthrate.
daily.example: It is truly regrettable that my old school is closing.

work.title: Thanking guests in a speech
work.description: Thanking attendees at a celebration.
work.example: We are deeply grateful that so many of you have joined us today.

work.title: Apologizing to a client
work.description: Expressing embarrassment over your own mistake.
work.example: I am truly embarrassed to have made such a basic mistake.

etymology: 「限り」 is the noun form of the verb 「限る」 and means “limit, end”. 「〜限りだ」 means “at the very limit of that feeling”, i.e. the emotion has reached its peak.

similar.title: 〜の極み
similar.explanation: 「の極み」 follows nouns (「感激の極み」) and is more literary. 「限りだ」 follows adjectives of emotion and is common in both everyday and formal settings.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: 「てたまらない」 stresses a feeling or physical sensation you can't hold back, and is conversational. 「限りだ」 is an exclamation about how you feel right now, and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜といったらない
similar.explanation: 「といったらない」 means something is beyond words, and can describe other people or things. 「限りだ」 only expresses the speaker's own feelings.

meaning: The moment one action happens, the next follows almost at the same time. Like “no sooner had ... than ...” or “as soon as ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form (た-form) + が早いか

senses.label: No sooner ... than ...
senses.meaning: Stresses an extremely short gap between two actions. Mostly describes things that already happened, so the second part is usually in the past tense. Gives a sense of eagerness or speed.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + が早いか + Verb た-form (e.g. 「言うが早いか」, 「着くが早いか」)
examples: The moment the kids got home, they tossed their school bags aside and ran off to play.
No sooner had the bell rung than he dashed out of the classroom.
The moment that shop opened, it was packed with customers.

notes: Written style, common in novels and narratives. The second part cannot be a command, intention, or request.
The subject is usually a third person; it describes someone else's actions.
In 「どちらが早いか比べる」, 「が早いか」 just means “which is faster”. That is not this pattern.

daily.title: Describing your child
daily.description: Telling a friend how hungry your son was.
daily.example: The second my son said 「いただきます」, he started shoveling down his food.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Describing a character's quick action.
daily.example: The man grabbed the wallet and vanished into the crowd in an instant.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a product selling out at launch.
work.example: The new model sold out the moment it was released.

etymology: Literally “which is faster, doing A or (doing B)?”. The two actions happen so quickly you can't tell which came first, hence “as soon as ...”.

similar.title: 〜や否や
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning; both are written style. 「や否や」 is stiffer; 「が早いか」 stresses quickness and eagerness.

similar.title: 〜なり (as soon as)
similar.explanation: 「なり」 is also used for a third person's past actions, and the second part is often unexpected. 「が早いか」 stresses that the two actions are almost simultaneous.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: 「たとたん」 is more conversational, and the second part is often something unexpected. 「が早いか」 is written style, and the second part is usually a deliberate action by the subject.

similar.title: 〜そばから
similar.explanation: 「そばから」 describes something that keeps happening: “no sooner ... than again ...”. 「が早いか」 describes a single sequence.

meaning: Once something happens, it inevitably leads to a result that can't be undone or stopped. Like “once ..., that's the end of it”.
connection: Verb た-form + が最後; Verb た-form + ら最後

senses.label: Once ..., it's all over
senses.meaning: 「〜たが最後」 means that once you do something, a bad, irreversible situation is sure to follow. Fairly literary.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + が最後 (e.g. 「見つかったが最後」, 「言ったが最後」)
examples: Once that person catches you, you'll be stuck listening to him for hours.
Once you say this secret out loud, there's no going back.

senses.label: (Casual) once ..., there's no stopping
senses.meaning: 「〜たら最後」 means the same and is more conversational. Often describes someone's habit: once they start something, they can't stop.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + ら最後 (e.g. 「寝たら最後」, 「飲んだら最後」)
examples: Once my dad falls asleep, nothing will wake him until morning.
Once he starts drinking, he won't come home until morning.
Once you start this game, you won't be able to stop.

notes: The second part is usually a bad, irreversible result, or a state of not being able to stop.
In 「これが最後だ」 (this is the last time), 「が最後」 is just the ordinary noun. That is not this pattern.
It always follows the た-form. 「〜たが最後」 is more literary than 「〜たら最後」.

daily.title: Warning a friend
daily.description: Telling a friend to steer clear of a pushy salesperson.
daily.example: Once you talk to that clerk, you'll get pushed into buying something.

daily.title: Complaining about your own habit
daily.description: Saying that once you sit down, you can't get up.
daily.example: Once I sit down on the sofa, I don't feel like doing anything anymore.

work.title: A senior colleague's warning
work.description: Reminding a newcomer how important trust is.
work.example: Once you lose people's trust, it's hard to win it back.

work.title: Security briefing
work.description: Explaining the risk of confidential information leaking.
work.example: Once information leaks online, it can never be completely erased.

etymology: 「最後」 here means “the end, it's over”. 「〜たが最後」 literally means “having done ..., that's the end”, so once it happens, there's no turning back.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うものなら
similar.explanation: 「ようものなら」 is a hypothetical warning about something that hasn't happened. 「が最後」 usually describes the inevitable result once something happens, and can also describe habits.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: 「たとたん」 only shows that one thing immediately follows another. 「が最後」 stresses that the result can't be undone or stopped.

similar.title: 〜ばそれまでだ
similar.explanation: 「ばそれまでだ」 means “if ..., everything is wasted” and focuses on “that's the end”. 「が最後」 focuses on falling into a situation you can't get out of.

meaning: Doing something while also serving a second purpose. Like “while ..., also ...” or “partly to ...”. Mostly used in letters and business settings.

senses.label: Also to ... (set phrase in letters)
senses.meaning: One action serves two purposes. The first is usually a courtesy, such as 「お礼」, 「ご挨拶」, 「お詫び」, or 「ご報告」. A set expression in business letters.
senses.connection: お礼／ご挨拶／お詫び／ご報告 + かたがた + 伺う／参上する etc.
examples: I will visit you soon to thank you and pay my respects.
Allow me first to report by letter, though informally, and also to make a request.

senses.label: While ..., also ...
senses.meaning: Also used in everyday contexts: while doing the first thing, you take care of the second. The first is often an action noun like 「散歩」 or 「見舞い」; the second is often movement like 「訪ねる」 or 「行く」.
senses.connection: 散歩／見舞い + かたがた + verb of movement
examples: While out for a walk, I stopped by the bookstore in front of the station.
While on a business trip, I visited a friend from my university days.

notes: The second part is usually a verb of movement or visiting, such as 「行く」, 「訪ねる」, or 「伺う」.
More formal than 「がてら」 and common in business letters. 「がてら」 is more everyday and conversational.
「〜の方々（かたがた）」 means “people, everyone”. That is not this pattern.

daily.title: Visiting a relative
daily.description: Visiting a relative in the hospital and stopping by your family home nearby.
daily.example: While visiting my aunt in the hospital, I stopped by my parents' home for the first time in a while.

daily.title: Reading a letter
daily.description: A seasonal greeting letter from a former teacher.
daily.example: Along with my summer greetings, let me tell you how I have been.

work.title: Business email
work.description: A newly assigned contact person reaches out to a client.
work.example: I would like to visit you to pay my respects and also to introduce my successor.

work.title: Apology visit
work.description: Apologizing to a client after an incident.
work.example: Regarding the recent matter, I have come to apologize and to explain what happened.

etymology: 「かたがた」 is written 「旁」 or 「旁々」. It originally meant “side, beside”, which extended to “at the same time, also”.

similar.title: 〜がてら
similar.explanation: 「がてら」 can follow the verb ます-stem and is more everyday. 「かたがた」 only follows nouns and is used in formal settings like business letters.

similar.title: 〜を兼ねて
similar.explanation: 「を兼ねて」 means one activity serves several purposes and has the widest range of use. 「かたがた」 stresses courteous purposes and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜ついでに
similar.explanation: 「ついでに」 stresses using the chance of the main task to do a minor one. With 「かたがた」, both purposes carry similar weight, and it is more formal.

meaning: While doing one's main job or activity, also doing another activity over a long period. Like “besides ...” or “alongside ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + かたわら; Noun + の + かたわら

senses.label: Alongside one's main work
senses.meaning: The first part is a main, long-term job or role; the second is a side job, hobby, or community activity. It describes a state over a period of time, not a one-time action.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + かたわら (e.g. 「会社に勤めるかたわら」, 「教えるかたわら」)
examples: Besides working at a company, he writes novels.
Besides doing the housework, my mother also takes part in local volunteer activities.

senses.label: Noun + のかたわら
senses.meaning: Follows a noun for work or study, with the same meaning. Common when introducing someone's background.
senses.connection: Noun (仕事・研究・学業 etc.) + の + かたわら
examples: Alongside his job, Mr. Tanaka enjoys farming on weekends.
Alongside her research, the professor has written many books for general readers.

notes: Both parts are activities that go on for a long time. It can't describe two actions at the same moment, like 「歌を歌うかたわら料理する」; for that, use 「ながら」.
「傍ら」 originally means “beside”. In 「子供の傍らに座る」 (sit beside the child), it is used for physical space. That is not this pattern.
Mostly used in writing, profiles, and news reports.

daily.title: Introducing a friend
daily.description: Introducing a multi-talented friend to someone.
daily.example: Besides working as a nurse, she's also active as a picture-book author.

daily.title: Reading a profile interview
daily.description: A magazine introduces a musician with a day job.
daily.example: Alongside his teaching job, he has kept his band going.

work.title: Speaker bio
work.description: Introducing a speaker's background.
work.example: Besides teaching at a university, Mr. Yamada also works as a corporate consultant.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a business owner who balances the company and community work.
work.example: Alongside running the company, the president has devoted himself to supporting local children.

etymology: 「かたわら」 is written 「傍ら」 and originally means “beside, near”. From physical “beside” it extended to “beside one's main work”, meaning doing something else on the side.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: 「ながら」 means doing two things at the same moment (studying while listening to music). 「かたわら」 means doing something else alongside a long-term main occupation.

similar.title: 〜かたがた
similar.explanation: 「かたがた」 means one action serves two purposes (お礼かたがた伺う). 「かたわら」 means two activities running in parallel over a long time.

similar.title: 〜一方（で）
similar.explanation: 「一方で」 can mean doing two things at once, or present a contrasting side. 「かたわら」 only means doing something besides one's main occupation.

similar.title: 〜つつ
similar.explanation: 「つつ」 is a written version of 「ながら」 and means simultaneous actions. 「かたわら」 stresses the relationship between a main job and a side activity.

meaning: While doing one thing, also doing another. Like “while I'm at it” or “taking the chance to ...”.
connection: Noun (action) + がてら; Verb ます-stem + がてら

senses.label: Noun + がてら
senses.meaning: The first part is usually an action noun like 「散歩」, 「買い物」, or 「花見」. While doing it, you also do the second thing. Relaxed and mostly everyday.
senses.connection: 散歩／買い物／見物／気分転換 + がてら
examples: I'm going for a walk and stopping by the convenience store.
While out shopping, I dropped into a newly opened café.
Shall we walk around outside a bit for a change of pace?

senses.label: Verb ます-stem + がてら
senses.meaning: Follows the verb ます-stem with the same meaning. The second part is usually a movement like 「行く」, 「寄る」, or 「歩く」.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem (送り・遊び・歩き) + がてら
examples: While seeing my friend off to the station, I stopped by a bookstore.
While out having fun, we toured a nearby museum.

notes: The second part is usually related to movement, such as 「行く」, 「寄る」, 「歩く」, or 「見る」.
Both activities carry similar weight. It feels more like “killing two birds with one stone” than 「ついでに」.
More casual and relaxed than 「かたがた」. Not used in very formal letters.

daily.title: Going out on the weekend
daily.description: Telling your family you're heading out for a bit.
daily.example: I'm biking to the library, and I'll get some exercise too.

daily.title: Inviting a friend
daily.description: Inviting a friend to see the cherry blossoms and eat together.
daily.example: Let's go see the cherry blossoms and have a bento lunch in the park.

daily.title: Reading a travel blog
daily.description: A blog describing a place visited along the way.
daily.example: While sightseeing, I enjoyed shopping at the local market.

work.title: Heading out on an errand
work.description: Telling a coworker your plans for going out.
work.example: I'm dropping off documents at the client's office and grabbing lunch while I'm out.

etymology: It is generally thought to come from the classical conjunctive particles 「がてり」 and 「がてら」, meaning “while also, at the same time”. From the medieval period on, it settled into the meaning “while one is at it”.

similar.title: 〜かたがた
similar.explanation: 「かたがた」 only follows nouns and is mostly used in business letters. 「がてら」 can follow the verb ます-stem and is more conversational.

similar.title: 〜ついでに
similar.explanation: With 「ついでに」, the first activity is the main one and the second is a minor extra. With 「がてら」, both carry similar weight.

similar.title: 〜を兼ねて
similar.explanation: 「を兼ねて」 means one activity serves several purposes, and works in speech and writing. 「がてら」 is more casual, and the second part is usually a movement.

meaning: You expected one thing, but the result turned out unexpectedly different. Like “I thought ..., but actually ...”.
connection: Plain form + と思いきや; Plain form + かと思いきや

senses.label: I thought ..., but
senses.meaning: The first part is the speaker's expectation; the second is the actual result, which goes against it. Sounds surprised. Mostly describes things that already happened.
senses.connection: Plain form (nouns and な-adjectives can drop 「だ」) + と思いきや
examples: I thought the exam would be easy, but it was surprisingly hard.
I thought I was already done, but more than half was still left.

senses.label: I wondered if ..., but
senses.meaning: 「かと思いきや」 adds 「か」: “I thought maybe ..., but in fact ...”. The expectation has a tone of guessing or wondering.
senses.connection: Plain form + かと思いきや
examples: I thought the rain had stopped, but it started again.
I was sure I'd get scolded, but I got praised instead.
I thought this would be a mild winter, but we got heavy snow in February.

notes: Only describes facts that already happened and went against expectations. The second part cannot be an intention or command.
Slightly literary, but also common in essays, news, and online articles.
「思いきや」 is a classical form and does not conjugate; you cannot say 「思いきやない」 and so on.

daily.title: Talking about a movie with a friend
daily.description: Saying the ending was unexpected.
daily.example: I thought it was going to have a happy ending, but the main character died at the end.

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Describing your father's unexpected reaction.
daily.example: I thought my dad would object, but he agreed right away.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report on a game's surprise ending.
daily.example: Victory seemed certain, but they suffered a shocking come-from-behind loss in the final match.

work.title: Reporting at work
work.description: Reporting an unexpected sales trend to your boss.
work.example: We assumed it was a product for young people, but it's actually selling well among seniors.

etymology: Formed from 「思い」 (the stem of 「思う」), the classical past auxiliary 「き」, and 「や」 (question or exclamation). Originally “Did I think ...? (but it wasn't so)”, which became “I thought ..., but”.

similar.title: 〜かと思うと・〜かと思ったら
similar.explanation: 「かと思ったら」 can mean “just as ..., then ...” or express surprise. 「と思いきや」 specifically means the result went against expectations, and is more literary.

similar.title: 〜のに (contrast)
similar.explanation: 「のに」 shows a result against expectations along with dissatisfaction. 「と思いきや」 focuses on surprise and doesn't necessarily imply complaint.

similar.title: 〜かと思う・〜かと思った
similar.explanation: 「かと思った」 only states what you expected. 「と思いきや」 must be followed by a fact that contradicts the expectation.

meaning: 「AもAならBもBだ」 means both A and B are at fault. 「AがAなら」 means “if A were the right kind of A”.
connection: Noun A + も（が） + Noun A + なら、Noun B + も + Noun B（だ）

senses.label: Both are just as bad
senses.meaning: 「AもAならBもBだ」 repeats each noun to criticize both A and B. Like “A is bad, and B is no better”. Sounds strongly critical or exasperated.
senses.connection: Noun A + も + Noun A + なら、Noun B + も + Noun B（だ） (e.g. 「親も親なら子も子だ」)
examples: The parents are bad, and so are the kids. Neither has any manners.
The husband is no better than the wife; both of them do nothing but waste money.
The store is bad, and the customers are no better.

senses.label: If A were the right A
senses.meaning: 「AがAなら」 repeats a noun to mean “if A were a (suitable) A”. Common in 「時代が時代なら」, implying things would turn out differently under different conditions.
senses.connection: Noun A + が + Noun A + なら (e.g. 「時代が時代なら」, 「親が親なら」)
examples: Had he been born in a different era, he probably would have become a hero.
Like parent, like child: neither of them listens to anyone.

notes: The same noun must be repeated, as in 「親も親」 or 「子も子」.
「AもAならBもBだ」 is for criticism and cannot be used for praise.
「時代が時代なら」 is a common set phrase with a regretful tone.

daily.title: Reading local news
daily.description: Reacting to news of parents covering for their child's misbehavior.
daily.example: With parents like that, they're all as bad as each other.

daily.title: Complaining about neighbors
daily.description: Commenting on a dispute between a landlord and a tenant.
daily.example: The landlord's bad and so is the tenant. You can't reason with either of them.

daily.title: Reading a historical novel
daily.description: The narrator laments that a character was born at the wrong time.
daily.example: In a different era, she might have become the leader of a nation.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator criticizes both the government and the media.
work.example: The government is bad, and the media are no better. Nobody wants to take responsibility.

work.title: Coworkers gossiping
work.description: Talking about a boss and subordinates blaming each other.
work.example: The boss is no better than the staff; they keep pushing mistakes onto each other.

etymology: Built from the particle 「も」 or 「が」, the conditional 「なら」, and a repeated noun. Repeating the noun stresses “that's just the kind of person they are”, which leads to criticism or a hypothetical.

similar.title: 〜も〜ば〜も
similar.explanation: Patterns like 「AもあればBもある」 simply list things, positive or negative. 「AもAならBもB」 is only for criticizing both sides.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: Ordinary 「なら」 marks a supposition or topic. This pattern repeats the same noun to express a judgment (“that's just how they are”) or regret.

meaning: Follows a number to stress how large the amount is. Like “a full ...”, “as much as ...”, or “upwards of ...”.
connection: Number + からある／からする／からの + Noun

senses.label: (Size) a full ...
senses.meaning: 「からある」 is used for weight, length, height, or size, stressing “a full ... or so”. Implies it may be even more.
senses.connection: Number (キロ・メートル・トン etc.) + からある + Noun
examples: He carried luggage weighing a good 30 kilos all by himself.
Apparently there are fish as long as two meters in the lake.

senses.label: (Price) as much as ...
senses.meaning: 「からする」 is used for prices, stressing “costing as much as ...”.
senses.connection: Amount (円・ドル etc.) + からする + Noun
examples: He owns several watches that cost upwards of a million yen.
I hear each of those paintings is worth tens of millions of yen.

senses.label: (Number of people etc.) as many as ...
senses.meaning: 「からの」 comes before a noun and is often used for numbers of people, quantities, or time, stressing “as many as ...”.
senses.connection: Number + からの + Noun
examples: As many as 50,000 spectators gathered at the venue.
This temple houses as many as a thousand Buddhist statues.

notes: It must follow a specific number, and one that feels large.
In 「昔からある店」 (a shop that has been there for ages) and 「1000円からのご注文」 (orders from 1,000 yen), 「から」 marks a starting point. That is not this pattern.
Prices usually take 「からする」, weight and length take 「からある」, and numbers of people before a noun usually take 「からの」.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: Talking about a big fish a family member caught.
daily.example: I heard my brother caught a sea bream a whole meter long.

daily.title: At a luxury store
daily.description: Shocked at the price of an item.
daily.example: This bag costs 500,000 yen or more. There's no way I can buy it.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report on a packed music festival.
daily.example: As many as 30,000 young people flocked to the outdoor festival.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting the scale of an accident.
work.example: At the accident site, steel beams weighing as much as 20 tons blocked the road.

work.title: Project briefing
work.description: Explaining how many users were affected.
work.example: This outage brought in as many as 10,000 inquiries.

etymology: 「から」 originally marks a starting point. “Number + から” means “from this amount (and up)”, i.e. “at least this much”, which came to stress how large the amount is.

similar.title: 〜も (emphasizing amount)
similar.explanation: 「三時間も」 shows the speaker feels the amount is large; it is widely used and conversational. 「からある」 stresses “at least this much” and is more literary.

similar.title: 〜にのぼる
similar.explanation: 「にのぼる」 means a total “reaches ...” and is usually a predicate in statistics. 「からある／からの」 usually modifies a noun.
